title: Day 50: Integrated Revision of Transport in Plants
introduction: This lesson provides a concise, NEET‑focused revision of all concepts related to transport in plants, linking fundamentals to high‑yield exam applications.

sections.heading: Overall Overview of Plant Transport
sections.content: Plant transport comprises water movement through the xylem and solute movement through the phloem, driven by gradients in water potential, pressure, and concentration. The two major pathways—apoplastic and symplastic—operate in roots, stems and leaves, integrating root pressure, transpiration pull, and the pressure‑flow mechanism to sustain growth and metabolism.
keyPoints: Xylem transports water and minerals; phloem transports organic solutes
Water movement follows water potential gradient (Ψw)
Apoplast = cell wall continuum; symplast = cytoplasmic continuum via plasmodesmata
neetTips: Memorise the direction of flow in xylem (upward) vs phloem (bidirectional)
Link each transport driver (root pressure, transpiration pull, pressure flow) to its physiological context

sections.heading: Diffusion vs Osmosis
sections.content: Diffusion is the net movement of solute molecules from higher to lower concentration without a semipermeable membrane, whereas osmosis is the diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane driven by water potential difference. Both are passive processes, but osmosis always involves water and a membrane.
keyPoints: Diffusion: solute movement, no membrane required
Osmosis: water movement, requires semipermeable membrane
Both are driven by concentration/water potential gradients
neetTips: Remember: Osmosis = diffusion of water only

sections.heading: Applying Water Potential (Ψw)
sections.content: Water potential (Ψw) = Ψs + Ψp, where Ψs is solute potential (negative) and Ψp is pressure potential (positive). Water moves from regions of higher (less negative) Ψw to lower (more negative) Ψw. In roots, Ψs is low due to mineral uptake, creating a gradient that draws water upward.
keyPoints: Ψw = Ψs + Ψp
Water moves from higher to lower Ψw
Root cells have low Ψs, high Ψp (turgor)
neetTips: When solving numerical problems, calculate Ψs = -iCRT and add any turgor pressure

sections.heading: Plasmolysis vs Turgidity
sections.content: Plasmolysis occurs when plant cells lose water in a hypertonic environment, causing the plasma membrane to detach from the cell wall. Turgidity is the opposite—water influx in a hypotonic medium generates turgor pressure that pushes the membrane against the wall, maintaining rigidity.
keyPoints: Plasmolysis: membrane pulls away, cell becomes flaccid
Turgidity: membrane pressed against wall, cell firm
neetTips: Link plasmolysis to loss of turgor in wilting plants

sections.heading: Apoplastic vs Symplastic Transport
sections.content: The apoplastic pathway follows the cell wall continuum and intercellular spaces, bypassing membranes, while the symplastic pathway moves through the cytoplasm interconnected by plasmodesmata. In roots, water initially follows the apoplast until the Casparian strip forces entry into the symplast.
keyPoints: Apoplast: cell walls, no membrane crossing
Symplast: cytoplasm, plasmodesmata
Casparian strip blocks apoplastic flow, forces symplastic entry
neetTips: NEET often asks which pathway is blocked by the Casparian strip

sections.heading: Root Pressure & Guttation
sections.content: Root pressure develops when active uptake of ions into the xylem lowers Ψs, causing water to enter osmotically and generate a positive pressure (up to 0.5 MPa). This pressure can exude water droplets (guttation) from leaf margins during low transpiration conditions.
keyPoints: Root pressure = osmotic entry of water into xylem
Positive pressure pushes water upward
Guttation occurs when transpiration is minimal
neetTips: Remember guttation occurs at night or high humidity, not to be confused with transpiration

sections.heading: Transpiration & Transpiration Pull
sections.content: Transpiration is the loss of water vapor from stomata, creating a negative pressure (tension) in the leaf xylem. This tension pulls water upward through the continuous water column—a process termed transpiration pull.
keyPoints: Transpiration creates negative pressure in leaf xylem
Transpiration pull = tension-driven upward movement
Rate depends on stomatal aperture, humidity, temperature
neetTips: Link high transpiration rates to increased leaf temperature and low humidity

sections.heading: Cohesion‑Tension Theory
sections.content: The cohesion‑tension theory explains how water ascends in the xylem: cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to vessel walls transmit the tension generated by transpiration throughout the column, preventing cavitation under normal conditions.
keyPoints: Cohesion: water‑water hydrogen bonds
Adhesion: water‑wall attraction
Tension transmitted without breakage
neetTips: NEET often asks why water can rise >100 m—cite cohesion‑tension

sections.heading: Regulation of Stomatal Aperture
sections.content: Stomata open in response to blue light, low internal CO₂, and high turgor in guard cells (K⁺ influx, water entry). They close under high CO₂, abscisic acid (ABA) signaling, drought, or darkness (K⁺ efflux, loss of turgor).
keyPoints: Blue light activates H⁺‑ATPase → K⁺ uptake → opening
ABA triggers K⁺ efflux → closure
Guard cell turgor dictates aperture
neetTips: Link ABA to drought‑induced stomatal closure

sections.heading: Xylem Anatomy and Function
sections.content: Xylem consists of tracheids (long, tapered cells with pits) and vessel elements (short, wide tubes with perforation plates). Both are dead at maturity, forming a continuous, lignified conduit for unidirectional water transport from roots to shoots.
keyPoints: Tracheids: narrow, pits, support
Vessels: wide, perforations, high conductivity
Both lack protoplasm, rely on cohesion‑tension
neetTips: NEET may ask which element provides greater hydraulic conductivity—vessels

sections.heading: Phloem Anatomy and Function
sections.content: Phloem comprises sieve‑tube elements (living, lack nucleus, contain sieve plates) and companion cells (metabolically active). Together they transport photosynthates from source (leaves) to sink (roots, fruits) via pressure‑flow.
keyPoints: Sieve tubes: porous end walls (sieve plates)
Companion cells: load/unload sugars
Transport is bidirectional
neetTips: Remember that phloem transport is driven by osmotic pressure differences

sections.heading: Pressure‑Flow (Mass‑Flow) Hypothesis
sections.content: At source tissues, sucrose loading lowers Ψs, causing water influx and raising turgor pressure (high Ψp). At sinks, sucrose unloading raises Ψs, water exits, lowering pressure. The resulting pressure gradient drives bulk flow of phloem sap.
keyPoints: Source: high pressure, sucrose loading
Sink: low pressure, sucrose unloading
Flow direction follows pressure gradient
neetTips: NEET often asks why phloem flow can be both upward and downward

sections.heading: Source‑Sink Dynamics
sections.content: Sources are mature photosynthetic tissues exporting assimilates; sinks are growing or storage organs importing them. The strength of a sink depends on its metabolic demand and ability to maintain low Ψs, influencing overall translocation rates.
keyPoints: Source: leaves, high photosynthesis
Sink: roots, fruits, tubers, growing buds
Sink strength = demand × low Ψs
neetTips: Link sink strength to fruit size and yield in exam scenarios

sections.heading: Mineral Uptake by Roots
sections.content: Minerals enter root cells via active transport (e.g., H⁺‑ATPase creates electrochemical gradient) or passive channels. Once inside, they move symplastically to the xylem, often coupled with water flow driven by transpiration pull.
keyPoints: H⁺‑ATPase establishes gradient for cation uptake
Passive channels allow anion influx
Minerals hitchhike with water in xylem
neetTips: Remember that nitrate uptake is often via H⁺ symport

sections.heading: Active vs Passive Transport Mechanisms
sections.content: Passive transport includes diffusion, facilitated diffusion, and osmosis—no energy required. Active transport uses ATP or ion gradients (primary or secondary) to move substances against their concentration gradient, essential for nutrient uptake and ion homeostasis.
keyPoints: Passive: down gradient, no ATP
Active primary: ATP‑driven pumps (e.g., H⁺‑ATPase)
Active secondary: uses existing gradient (symport/antiport)
neetTips: NEET may ask which transport is used for K⁺ uptake in roots—primary active

sections.heading: Key NCERT Diagrams to Remember
sections.content: Important diagrams include: (1) Xylem and phloem cross‑section of a stem, (2) Water potential diagram showing Ψs and Ψp components, (3) Stomatal opening mechanism with guard cell ion fluxes, (4) Pressure‑flow model illustrating source‑sink pressure gradient.
keyPoints: Stem cross‑section: label tracheids, vessels, sieve tubes, companion cells
Water potential diagram: Ψw = Ψs + Ψp
Stomatal diagram: H⁺‑ATPase, K⁺ influx
neetTips: Practice redrawing these diagrams; NEET often asks line‑based questions

sections.heading: Numerical Problems on Transport
sections.content: Typical calculations involve water potential (Ψs = –iCRT), root pressure magnitude, or pressure differences required for phloem flow. Apply the formula ΔP = RTΔC for osmotic pressure and use Ψw gradients to predict water movement direction.
keyPoints: Ψs = –iCRT (i = van’t Hoff factor)
Root pressure ≈ osmotic pressure of xylem sap
Phloem flow pressure ≈ ΔΨp between source and sink
neetTips: Convert all units to SI before plugging into formulas

sections.heading: Frequent Pitfalls in Transport Questions
sections.content: Mistakes include confusing apoplastic vs symplastic routes, mixing up root pressure with transpiration pull, assuming phloem flow is unidirectional, and overlooking the role of the Casparian strip. Also, misreading water potential signs leads to wrong direction predictions.
keyPoints: Apoplast blocked by Casparian strip
Root pressure ≠ transpiration pull
Phloem flow can be bidirectional
Sign of Ψs is negative
neetTips: Read the question stem carefully for direction cues

sections.heading: Integrated Revision Practice
sections.content: Combine concepts: Analyze a scenario where a plant experiences drought, high temperature, and high soil salinity. Predict changes in Ψw, stomatal behavior, root pressure, and phloem loading. Use the cohesion‑tension theory to explain reduced transpiration pull and increased risk of cavitation.
keyPoints: Drought → lower Ψw, stomatal closure, reduced transpiration pull
Salinity → more negative Ψs, higher osmotic uptake cost
High temperature → increased transpiration rate if stomata open
neetTips: Link each environmental factor to at least two transport mechanisms for full marks

learningOutcome: Recall the structure and function of xylem and phloem
Differentiate between apoplastic and symplastic pathways
Apply water potential concepts to predict water movement
Explain the cohesion‑tension theory and pressure‑flow hypothesis
Identify common NEET traps and avoid them in answer writing

mcqs.question: A plant cell has a solute potential of –0.35 MPa and a pressure potential of +0.15 MPa. What is the water potential of the cell?
mcqs.explanation: Water potential (ψ) = solute potential (ψs) + pressure potential (ψp). Thus ψ = –0.35 MPa + 0.15 MPa = –0.20 MPa.

mcqs.question: Which of the following correctly describes the apoplast pathway for mineral ion movement in roots?
options: Movement through the cytoplasm connected by plasmodesmata
Movement across the plasma membrane into the symplast
Movement through cell walls and intercellular spaces without crossing membranes
Active transport via carrier proteins in the plasma membrane
mcqs.explanation: In the apoplast pathway, solutes travel extracellularly through cell walls and intercellular spaces, never crossing a membrane.

mcqs.question: According to the cohesion‑tension theory, which factor does NOT directly influence the magnitude of the transpiration pull?
mcqs.explanation: Root pressure is a separate mechanism that can push water upward but does not affect the tension generated by transpiration pull.

mcqs.question: In the pressure‑flow hypothesis, sugars move from source to sink because:
options: Higher hydrostatic pressure at the sink draws sugars
Higher solute concentration at the source creates an osmotic gradient
Active loading at the sink pushes sugars upward
mcqs.explanation: Loading of sugars at the source raises its osmotic potential, causing water influx, raising turgor pressure, and driving bulk flow toward the sink where pressure is lower.

mcqs.question: Guttation is most likely to be observed when:
options: Transpiration rate is high and soil moisture is low
Transpiration rate is low, humidity is high, and soil moisture is abundant
Stomata are fully open during midday
mcqs.explanation: Guttation occurs when transpiration is minimal (high humidity, low light) but root pressure is high, forcing water out through hydathodes.

mcqs.question: During plasmolysis, the plant cell's protoplast:
options: Detaches from the cell wall and shrinks
Remains unchanged while the cell wall expands
Lyses due to excess water intake
mcqs.explanation: In a hypertonic external solution, water leaves the cell, the protoplast contracts and pulls away from the rigid cell wall.

mcqs.question: Which plant hormone is primarily responsible for stomatal closure during drought stress?
mcqs.explanation: Abscisic acid (ABA) accumulates under water deficit and triggers guard‑cell signaling that closes stomata to conserve water.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes xylem vessels from tracheids?
options: Vessels have pits, tracheids lack pits
Vessels are shorter and have end walls with perforations, tracheids are longer and have tapered ends
Vessels conduct only water, tracheids conduct both water and sugars
Vessels are present only in gymnosperms, tracheids only in angiosperms
mcqs.explanation: Vessels are typically short, wide cells with perforated end walls, whereas tracheids are elongated, tapered, and lack perforations, relying on pits for water movement.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes diffusion from osmosis?
options: Diffusion is the movement of solute particles from higher to lower concentration, whereas osmosis is the movement of water across a semipermeable membrane from lower to higher water potential.
Diffusion requires a semipermeable membrane, while osmosis does not require any membrane.
Diffusion is an active transport process, whereas osmosis is a passive transport process.
Diffusion occurs only in gases and osmosis only in liquids.
mcqs.explanation: Diffusion involves net movement of any solute down its concentration gradient without the need for a membrane, while osmosis specifically refers to the passive movement of water through a semipermeable membrane from a region of higher water potential to lower water potential.

mcqs.question: When a plant cell is placed in a hypertonic solution, which process primarily causes plasmolysis?
options: Diffusion of solutes into the cell
Osmosis of water out of the cell
Active transport of ions out of the cell
Facilitated diffusion of sugars into the cell
mcqs.explanation: In a hypertonic external solution, water moves out of the cell by osmosis, leading to loss of turgor and separation of the plasma membrane from the cell wall (plasmolysis).

mcqs.question: The rate of diffusion of a gas across a membrane is directly proportional to which factor?
options: Square root of the gas's molecular weight
mcqs.explanation: According to Fick's law, the diffusion rate increases with a larger concentration gradient, assuming other factors such as temperature and membrane characteristics remain constant.

mcqs.question: Which statement about water potential (Ψ) is true in the context of osmosis?
options: Water moves from lower Ψ to higher Ψ
Water moves from higher Ψ to lower Ψ
Ψ is irrelevant for diffusion of gases
Ψ is always positive in plant cells
mcqs.explanation: Water always moves spontaneously from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential until equilibrium is reached.

mcqs.question: Two solutions are separated by a semipermeable membrane: Solution A contains 0.2 M sucrose and Solution B contains 0.2 M glucose. What is the net movement of water?
options: No net water movement because solute concentrations are equal
Water moves from A to B because sucrose molecules are larger
Water moves from B to A because glucose molecules are smaller
Water moves equally in both directions due to equal osmotic pressure
mcqs.explanation: Osmotic pressure depends on the total concentration of solute particles, not on their size; equal molar concentrations give equal osmotic pressures, so there is no net water flow.

mcqs.question: Which factor does NOT affect the rate of osmosis across a plant cell membrane?
options: Molecular weight of the solute particles
mcqs.explanation: Osmosis is driven by water potential differences; the molecular weight of the solute influences colligative properties but does not directly alter the rate of water movement across the membrane.

mcqs.question: In comparing diffusion and osmosis, which statement about the role of a semipermeable membrane is accurate?
options: Both diffusion and osmosis require a semipermeable membrane
Only diffusion requires a semipermeable membrane
Only osmosis requires a semipermeable membrane
mcqs.explanation: Diffusion can occur in any medium without a membrane, whereas osmosis specifically involves water moving through a semipermeable membrane that blocks solute passage.

mcqs.question: Soil water potential is –0.2 MPa and the water potential of a root cell is –0.4 MPa. In which direction will water move?
options: From soil into the root cell
From the root cell into the soil
mcqs.explanation: Water moves from a region of higher (less negative) water potential to lower (more negative) water potential; –0.2 MPa > –0.4 MPa, so water enters the root.

mcqs.question: A plant cell has a solute (osmotic) potential of –0.3 MPa and a pressure potential of +0.5 MPa. What is the overall water potential of the cell?
mcqs.explanation: Water potential ψ = ψs + ψp = –0.3 MPa + 0.5 MPa = +0.2 MPa.

mcqs.question: Which condition most directly leads to guttation in a plant?
options: High transpiration rate during the day
High root pressure combined with high night humidity
mcqs.explanation: Guttation occurs mainly at night when transpiration is low and root pressure builds up, forcing water out through hydathodes.

mcqs.question: In a leaf, the water potential of mesophyll cells is –0.9 MPa while that of guard cells is –0.6 MPa. What is the expected effect on stomatal aperture?
options: Stomata will close because water moves from guard cells to mesophyll
Stomata will open because water moves into guard cells
Stomata will open only if light is present
mcqs.explanation: Water moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) potential; it enters guard cells (–0.6 MPa → –0.9 MPa), increasing turgor and opening the stomata.

mcqs.question: A plant cell is placed in 0.2 M sucrose solution (solute potential ≈ –0.5 MPa). If the cell’s pressure potential is +0.3 MPa, what is the net water potential of the cell?
mcqs.explanation: ψ = ψs + ψp = –0.5 MPa + 0.3 MPa = –0.2 MPa.

mcqs.question: Which mechanism best explains the ascent of sap in tall trees despite gravity?
mcqs.explanation: The cohesion‑tension theory describes how transpiration creates a continuous water column pulled upward by cohesion and tension.

mcqs.question: A plant cell in a hypotonic solution has a water potential of –0.1 MPa, while the external solution has –0.4 MPa. What will happen to the cell?
options: It will gain turgor and become turgid
It will lose water and shrink
mcqs.explanation: Water moves from higher (–0.1 MPa) to lower (–0.4 MPa) potential, entering the cell, increasing turgor and making it turgid.

mcqs.question: What is the primary cause of plasmolysis in a plant cell placed in a hypertonic solution?
options: Influx of water into the cell
Efflux of water from the cell
Synthesis of new cell wall material
mcqs.explanation: In a hypertonic solution, the external solute concentration is higher than inside the cell, causing water to move out (efflux) by osmosis, leading to shrinkage of the protoplast (plasmolysis).

mcqs.question: In a turgid plant cell, the pressure potential (Ψp) is:
mcqs.explanation: Turgor pressure develops when water enters the cell, exerting a positive pressure against the cell wall; thus the pressure potential is positive in a turgid cell.

mcqs.question: Which statement is true regarding reversible plasmolysis?
options: The plasma membrane remains attached to the cell wall after plasmolysis
The cell wall collapses during plasmolysis
The protoplast cannot regain its original volume even after transfer to a hypotonic solution
Reversible plasmolysis occurs only in animal cells
mcqs.explanation: In reversible plasmolysis, the plasma membrane detaches from the wall but stays close enough to reattach when water re-enters; the cell wall itself does not collapse.

mcqs.question: Guard cells become turgid and open the stomata when placed in a solution with water potential –0.02 MPa, while surrounding epidermal cells have water potential –0.08 MPa. What is the direction of water movement?
options: From guard cells to epidermal cells
From epidermal cells to guard cells
From both cell types to the apoplast
mcqs.explanation: Water moves from higher (less negative) water potential to lower (more negative) potential; therefore it flows from guard cells (–0.02 MPa) to epidermal cells (–0.08 MPa).

mcqs.question: Which condition is most likely to cause irreversible plasmolysis in a leaf cell?
options: Exposure to 0.2 M sucrose for 5 min
Exposure to 0.5 M NaCl for 30 min
Exposure to distilled water for 10 min
Exposure to isotonic 0.3 M mannitol for 2 min
mcqs.explanation: A high concentration of NaCl for a prolonged period creates a strong hypertonic environment, leading to extensive loss of water and damage to the plasma membrane, making plasmolysis irreversible.

mcqs.question: In a turgid plant cell, water potential (Ψw) = –0.03 MPa and solute potential (Ψs) = –0.08 MPa. What is the pressure potential (Ψp)?
mcqs.explanation: Using Ψw = Ψs + Ψp, we get Ψp = Ψw – Ψs = –0.03 – (–0.08) = +0.05 MPa, a positive pressure potential indicating turgidity.

mcqs.question: Why does a plant cell not burst when placed in a hypotonic solution?
options: The rigid cell wall limits expansion
The plasma membrane is impermeable to water
The vacuole contracts to reduce volume
Active transport pumps out excess water
mcqs.explanation: The cellulose cell wall provides mechanical support and resists excessive expansion, preventing the cell from bursting despite the influx of water that creates turgor pressure.

mcqs.question: In root tissues, which description correctly defines the apoplastic pathway for water movement?
options: Movement through the cytoplasm via plasmodesmata
Movement through cell walls and intercellular spaces
Active transport across the plasma membrane
mcqs.explanation: The apoplastic pathway involves the passive flow of water and dissolved solutes through the cell walls and the extracellular spaces without crossing any plasma membranes.

mcqs.question: What is the primary function of the Casparian strip in the root endodermis?
options: It is present in the endodermis and blocks apoplastic flow
It is located in the pericycle
It allows free diffusion of solutes
mcqs.explanation: The Casparian strip is a band of suberin in the endodermal cell walls that forces water and solutes to cross the plasma membrane, thereby converting apoplastic flow to symplastic flow before entering the stele.

mcqs.question: The bulk movement of photosynthates from mesophyll cells to the phloem loading sites occurs mainly through which pathway?
mcqs.explanation: Sugars move from mesophyll to companion cells primarily via plasmodesmata, i.e., the symplastic route, allowing efficient loading into the phloem.

mcqs.question: Which statement about the symplastic pathway is FALSE?
options: It is restricted by the Casparian strip
It allows selective transport of ions via membrane carriers
It involves movement through the cytoplasm of cells
mcqs.explanation: The symplastic pathway bypasses the Casparian strip because transport occurs through the cytoplasm connected by plasmodesmata, not through the cell wall where the strip is located.

mcqs.question: During the initial uptake of mineral ions from the soil, the ions first travel through which pathway to reach the root cortex?
mcqs.explanation: Ions dissolve in the soil solution and first move radially inward through the cell walls and intercellular spaces, i.e., the apoplastic pathway, before crossing membranes into the cortex.

mcqs.question: Under conditions of high transpiration demand, which factor most directly increases the contribution of the symplastic pathway to water transport in roots?
mcqs.explanation: A greater number of plasmodesmata provides more cytoplasmic continuity, enhancing symplastic flow, especially when rapid water movement is required.

mcqs.question: In a dye‑tracing experiment, a water‑soluble dye applied to the root surface appears in the stele after a short period. Through which pathway did the dye most likely travel to reach the stele?
mcqs.explanation: The dye moves apoplastically until it reaches the Casparian strip, where it must cross the plasma membrane; thereafter it proceeds symplastically through plasmodesmata into the stele.

mcqs.question: Which of the following best describes the primary mechanism that generates root pressure in most herbaceous plants?
options: Active uptake of mineral ions into the xylem followed by water influx
Cohesive pull of the water column due to transpiration
Capillary rise of water in narrow xylem vessels
Osmotic movement of water from leaves to roots
mcqs.explanation: Root pressure arises when roots actively transport ions (e.g., K+, Na+) into the xylem, lowering its water potential and causing water to enter osmotically, generating a positive pressure.

mcqs.question: Root pressure is most commonly observed under which environmental condition?
options: High soil moisture with low atmospheric demand
mcqs.explanation: When soil is water‑logged and atmospheric demand is low (e.g., at night), water can enter the xylem by osmosis, producing measurable root pressure.

mcqs.question: Guttation droplets are primarily composed of:
options: Water with high concentrations of sugars
mcqs.explanation: Guttation exudes xylem sap that contains mineral ions absorbed by the roots; the droplets are therefore a dilute solution of these ions.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly differentiates root pressure from transpiration pull?
options: Root pressure moves water upward only in the presence of leaves
Transpiration pull can operate in the absence of root pressure
Both mechanisms rely on active transport of solutes
Root pressure is generated by capillary action
mcqs.explanation: Transpiration pull (cohesion‑tension) depends on water loss from leaves and can function without any root‑generated pressure, whereas root pressure is independent of leaf transpiration.

mcqs.question: In a tall tree, root pressure is insufficient to raise water to the top because:
options: The osmotic potential of xylem sap is too low
The magnitude of root pressure rarely exceeds about 0.2 MPa
Cohesion of water is lost at great height
mcqs.explanation: Measured root pressures are usually ≤0.2 MPa, far below the pressure needed to lift water several tens of meters; tall trees rely on transpiration pull instead.

mcqs.question: Which experimental observation would directly indicate the presence of root pressure in a potted plant?
options: Wilting of leaves during the day
Exudation of sap from a cut stem at night
Rapid closure of stomata under high CO₂
mcqs.explanation: If a cut stem or decapitated shoot exudes clear sap during the night, it reflects a positive pressure generated by the roots.

mcqs.question: The magnitude of root pressure is directly proportional to:
options: The concentration gradient of mineral ions between soil and xylem
mcqs.explanation: Root pressure depends on active ion uptake; a larger concentration difference between soil solution and xylem sap drives greater osmotic influx of water, increasing pressure.

mcqs.question: Which of the following best describes transpiration pull?
options: Upward movement of water due to negative pressure generated by evaporation at leaf surfaces
Active uptake of water by root hairs
mcqs.explanation: Transpiration pull is created by the loss of water vapour from mesophyll cells, generating a negative pressure (tension) that pulls the continuous water column upward through the xylem.

mcqs.question: According to the cohesion‑tension theory, the primary force that maintains continuity of the water column in xylem is:
options: Adhesion of water molecules to vessel walls
mcqs.explanation: Cohesion between water molecules allows the column to transmit the tension generated at the leaf surface throughout the xylem without breaking.

mcqs.question: Which factor does NOT increase the rate of transpiration?
mcqs.explanation: Elevated CO₂ causes partial stomatal closure, reducing stomatal aperture and thus decreasing transpiration rate.

mcqs.question: In a well‑watered plant, the water potential at the leaf surface is –0.1 MPa and in the root xylem is –0.02 MPa. Water moves primarily from:
mcqs.explanation: Water moves from regions of higher (less negative) water potential to lower (more negative) potential; thus it flows from the root xylem (–0.02 MPa) toward the leaf (–0.1 MPa).

mcqs.question: Which statement about stomatal regulation during transpiration is FALSE?
options: Guard cells swell when K⁺ ions enter, opening the pore
Abscisic acid induces stomatal closure during drought
Light of wavelength 700 nm is most effective in opening stomata
High internal CO₂ concentration promotes stomatal closure
mcqs.explanation: Blue light (≈450 nm) is most effective in activating the photoreceptors that open stomata; red light (≈700 nm) is far less effective.

mcqs.question: The term "transpiration stream" refers to:
options: The flow of sugars in phloem
The upward movement of water and dissolved minerals in xylem
The downward movement of water in phloem
The movement of gases through stomata
mcqs.explanation: Transpiration stream denotes the continuous upward flow of water, carrying mineral nutrients, driven by transpiration pull in the xylem.

mcqs.question: Which experimental observation supports the existence of transpiration pull?
options: Cutting a stem near the tip stops water movement above the cut
Water rises higher in a narrow capillary tube than in a wide one
Xylem vessels can transport water when the plant is placed in a vacuum
Roots exude guttation droplets at night
mcqs.explanation: When a stem is cut above the point of water ascent, the tension in the water column is released, and water movement above the cut ceases, demonstrating that a continuous column under tension (transpiration pull) is required.

mcqs.question: Which of the following best describes the primary driving force behind upward movement of water in the cohesion‑tension theory?
mcqs.explanation: Transpiration from stomata creates a water potential gradient that generates negative pressure (tension) in the leaf xylem, pulling water upward through the continuous column.

mcqs.question: In cohesion‑tension theory, the cohesion property of water is due to which type of intermolecular force?
mcqs.explanation: Water molecules are attracted to each other by hydrogen bonds, providing the cohesion needed to transmit tension throughout the xylem column.

mcqs.question: Which condition most directly leads to cavitation (air embolism) in the xylem according to cohesion‑tension theory?
options: Excessive tension (negative pressure) due to rapid water loss
mcqs.explanation: When transpiration is very rapid, the resulting high tension can exceed the tensile strength of water, causing the column to break and form air bubbles (cavitation).

mcqs.question: According to cohesion‑tension theory, why does water move from the leaf mesophyll to the atmosphere?
options: Higher water potential in the atmosphere
Lower water potential in the leaf intercellular spaces
Higher solute concentration in the atmosphere
mcqs.explanation: Water evaporates from the moist mesophyll into the drier intercellular air spaces, creating a lower (more negative) water potential that drives diffusion to the atmosphere.

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding the cohesion‑tension mechanism?
options: Water columns in xylem are continuous from roots to leaves
Tension in the xylem is a positive pressure
Cohesion allows transmission of tension throughout the column
Transpiration creates a water potential gradient
mcqs.explanation: Tension in the xylem is a negative pressure (suction), not a positive pressure; the other statements are true.

mcqs.question: In a tall tree, the water potential at the top of the xylem is approximately –0.2 MPa while at the roots it is –0.02 MPa. What is the approximate tension (negative pressure) experienced in the xylem column?
mcqs.explanation: Tension equals the difference in water potential (ψ_top – ψ_root) = –0.2 MPa – (–0.02 MPa) = –0.18 MPa, indicating a negative pressure of 0.18 MPa.

mcqs.question: Which anatomical feature of xylem vessels most enhances the efficiency of the cohesion‑tension mechanism?
mcqs.explanation: Lignified vessels with relatively wide diameters provide low resistance and structural strength, allowing the transmission of tension without collapse, which is essential for the cohesion‑tension process.

mcqs.question: Which ion is primarily taken up by guard cells during stomatal opening?
mcqs.explanation: Guard cells accumulate K⁺ ions, which lowers their membrane potential, draws in Cl⁻ and malate, and creates an osmotic gradient that leads to water influx and turgor increase, opening the stomatal pore.

mcqs.question: Blue light induces stomatal opening mainly by activating which of the following in guard cells?
mcqs.explanation: Blue light activates phototropins, which trigger phosphorylation of the plasma‑membrane H⁺‑ATPase. The resulting hyperpolarization drives K⁺ influx, increasing guard‑cell turgor and opening the stomata.

mcqs.question: Abscisic acid (ABA) causes stomatal closure primarily through an increase in which secondary messenger inside guard cells?
mcqs.explanation: ABA perception leads to the production of reactive oxygen species and elevation of cytosolic Ca²⁺, which activates ion channels that release K⁺ and Cl⁻, reducing guard‑cell turgor and closing the stomata.

mcqs.question: An increase in intercellular CO₂ concentration from 200 to 600 µmol mol⁻¹ will most likely cause which change in stomatal aperture?
mcqs.explanation: Elevated internal CO₂ is sensed by guard cells, leading to activation of Ca²⁺‑dependent K⁺ efflux channels, loss of turgor and closure of the stomatal pore.

mcqs.question: Which environmental condition most directly leads to reduced stomatal conductance?
mcqs.explanation: Low atmospheric humidity raises transpiration demand, causing leaf water potential to become more negative; guard cells lose turgor to limit water loss, thereby reducing stomatal conductance.

mcqs.question: During stomatal opening, the primary role of potassium channels in guard cells is to:
options: Allow K⁺ efflux causing loss of turgor
Allow K⁺ influx leading to osmotic water uptake
mcqs.explanation: Opening‑type K⁺ channels permit K⁺ influx, increasing the solute concentration inside guard cells, which draws water osmotically, raises turgor, and opens the stomatal pore.

mcqs.question: In the cohesion‑tension theory, stomatal closure affects the tension in the xylem column primarily by:
options: Increasing tension in the xylem column
Decreasing tension in the xylem column
Reversing the direction of water flow
mcqs.explanation: When stomata close, transpiration rate drops, reducing the pulling force (tension) generated in the xylem; thus the tension in the water column decreases.

mcqs.question: Which xylem cell type is primarily responsible for long-distance water transport in most angiosperms?
mcqs.explanation: Vessel elements are wide, short cells with perforated end walls that form continuous tubes, allowing efficient bulk flow of water in angiosperms.

mcqs.question: Lateral movement of water between adjacent xylem vessels is facilitated by which structure?
mcqs.explanation: Pits are thin areas in the secondary wall that lack lignified material, permitting water to pass laterally between neighboring vessels.

mcqs.question: According to the cohesion‑tension theory, the negative pressure (tension) that pulls water upward in the xylem is generated mainly by:
options: Active uptake of ions in roots
mcqs.explanation: Transpiration creates a water potential gradient; loss of water from leaf stomata generates tension that is transmitted down the continuous water column.

mcqs.question: Which statement about root pressure is correct?
options: It can push water up to the tops of tall trees
It is generated by active uptake of K⁺ ions in the root cortex
It occurs mainly at night when transpiration is low
It is responsible for the cohesion of water molecules
mcqs.explanation: Root pressure builds up when ions are actively accumulated in the xylem at night, creating a positive pressure that can exude water through guttation but cannot lift water to great heights.

mcqs.question: In xylem physiology, "embolism" refers to:
options: Blockage of vessels by air bubbles
Formation of lignin in cell walls
mcqs.explanation: Embolism is the formation of air bubbles that interrupt the continuous water column, reducing hydraulic conductivity.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes primary from secondary xylem?
options: Primary xylem contains vessels, secondary xylem contains only tracheids
Primary xylem is formed during primary growth, secondary xylem is added by the vascular cambium
Primary xylem transports sugars, secondary xylem transports water
Primary xylem is located in the pith, secondary xylem in the cortex
mcqs.explanation: Primary xylem is produced by the apical meristem during elongation; secondary xylem is produced laterally by the vascular cambium, increasing stem girth.

mcqs.question: In a typical dicot stem, the arrangement of vascular tissues in a bundle is:
mcqs.explanation: In dicot stems, each vascular bundle has xylem positioned toward the interior (adaxial side) and phloem toward the exterior (abaxial side).

mcqs.question: Which cell type in the phloem is living and contains numerous mitochondria to provide energy for active transport of sugars?
mcqs.explanation: Companion cells are living, rich in mitochondria and supply ATP for active loading of sucrose into sieve tube elements.

mcqs.question: According to the pressure‑flow hypothesis, what is the primary driving force for bulk flow of assimilates in the phloem?
options: Osmotic pressure gradient between source and sink
mcqs.explanation: A higher osmotic pressure at the source draws water in, raising turgor, while lower pressure at the sink creates a pressure gradient that drives bulk flow.

mcqs.question: In phloem loading of a source leaf that uses active apoplastic loading, which of the following occurs?
options: Sucrose diffuses passively into sieve elements
Sucrose is pumped into companion cells via H⁺‑sucrose symport
Water moves out of phloem causing turgor loss
Sucrose is polymerized into starch within sieve tubes
mcqs.explanation: Active apoplastic loading involves H⁺‑sucrose symporters in companion cell membranes that use ATP‑generated proton gradients to import sucrose against its concentration gradient.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes phloem from xylem?
options: Phloem cells are dead at maturity
Xylem conducts sugars from source to sink
mcqs.explanation: Phloem conducts photosynthates (mainly sugars) in both directions depending on source‑sink relationships, whereas xylem mainly moves water and minerals upward.

mcqs.question: The presence of which structure in sieve tube elements facilitates the rapid movement of solutes between adjacent cells?
mcqs.explanation: Sieve plates contain numerous plasmodesmata that allow continuous cytoplasmic connections for fast solute flow between sieve elements.

mcqs.question: During phloem unloading at a sink tissue that relies on symplastic unloading, which process predominates?
options: Polymerization of sucrose into starch within sieve element
mcqs.explanation: Symplastic unloading uses plasmodesmatal connections for sucrose to diffuse directly into sink cells without crossing a membrane.

mcqs.question: Which component is NOT typically found in phloem sap?
mcqs.explanation: Phloem sap contains soluble substances like sugars, ions, and amino acids; lignin is a structural polymer present in cell walls, not in the sap.

mcqs.question: According to the pressure‑flow hypothesis, what creates the bulk flow of solutes in the phloem?
options: Osmotic pressure gradient between source and sink
mcqs.explanation: Active loading of sugars at the source raises the osmotic potential, drawing water in and generating high turgor pressure; unloading at the sink lowers pressure, establishing a pressure gradient that drives bulk flow.

mcqs.question: In many plants, sucrose is actively loaded into sieve elements at the source. Which cell type is primarily responsible for this active loading?
mcqs.explanation: Companion cells are closely associated with sieve elements and use ATP‑dependent transporters to load sucrose, creating the high osmotic potential needed for pressure generation.

mcqs.question: If a phloem strand is cut above a source leaf, what will happen to the movement of sugars?
options: Flow reverses toward the cut end
Flow increases in the remaining segment
mcqs.explanation: Cutting above the source eliminates the high‑pressure region that drives the flow; without the pressure gradient, translocation ceases in that segment.

mcqs.question: Which statement about the energy requirement of the pressure‑flow mechanism is correct?
options: Both loading and unloading are passive
Loading is active, unloading is passive
Both loading and unloading are active
No energy is required at any stage
mcqs.explanation: Sucrose loading at the source generally requires active transport (ATP), whereas unloading at many sinks can occur passively as the concentration gradient falls.

mcqs.question: During the day, a mature leaf acts as a source. Which change in phloem turgor pressure is expected compared to night when the leaf becomes a sink?
options: Turgor pressure is zero at night
mcqs.explanation: Daytime photosynthesis produces sucrose, which is loaded into the phloem, raising osmotic potential and turgor pressure; at night the leaf imports sugars, lowering its turgor.

mcqs.question: The rate of phloem translocation is most directly affected by which physical factor?
mcqs.explanation: According to Hagen‑Poiseuille’s law, flow rate is inversely proportional to the viscosity of the sap; higher viscosity (e.g., due to concentrated sugars) reduces the speed of bulk flow.

mcqs.question: According to the pressure‑flow hypothesis, which outcome would NOT be expected from a mutation that eliminates active sucrose loading in source leaves?
options: Reduced turgor pressure in sieve tubes at source
Accumulation of sugars in the source leaf
mcqs.explanation: Without active loading, the pressure gradient cannot be established, so transport rate would fall, not increase; the other options are direct consequences of impaired loading.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly describes the source in the source‑sink relationship of phloem transport?
options: Mature photosynthetic leaves during the day
mcqs.explanation: Source tissues are those that produce and export assimilates, primarily mature leaves that photosynthesize during daylight.

mcqs.question: According to the pressure‑flow hypothesis, the primary driving force for bulk flow in the phloem is:
options: Active uptake of K+ in sieve tubes
Osmotic water influx due to sucrose loading at the source
Transpirational pull generated in the xylem
Root pressure generated in the root hairs
mcqs.explanation: Sucrose loading at the source raises osmotic potential, causing water to enter, increasing turgor pressure that drives flow toward the sink.

mcqs.question: Girdling a stem above a developing tuber will most likely cause which immediate effect on the tuber?
mcqs.explanation: Girdling blocks phloem transport away from the tuber, causing sugars to accumulate in the tuber, enhancing its sink strength.

mcqs.question: During the night, the predominant direction of phloem transport in most plants is:
mcqs.explanation: At night, leaves are not photosynthesizing and act as sinks, while roots export stored carbohydrates, reversing the daytime flow.

mcqs.question: Fruits become strong sinks during ripening mainly because:
options: Increased expression of sucrose‑H+ symporters in phloem parenchyma
Closure of stomata reduces water loss
mcqs.explanation: Ripening fruits up‑regulate sucrose‑H+ symporters, enhancing active loading of sucrose from the phloem, thereby increasing sink strength.

mcqs.question: In a plant that loads sucrose into the phloem exclusively via the apoplastic pathway, which component is essential to maintain the source‑sink gradient?
options: Energy‑dependent sucrose‑H+ symporters at the source
Passive diffusion of sucrose through plasmodesmata
High turgor pressure in the sink tissues
Root pressure generated in the root tip
mcqs.explanation: Apoplastic loading requires active sucrose‑H+ symporters to accumulate sucrose against its concentration gradient, creating the osmotic pressure difference.

mcqs.question: A shaded leaf that is not photosynthetically active will function as:
mcqs.explanation: Without photosynthesis, the leaf consumes stored carbohydrates, acting as a sink that imports assimilates from other source tissues.

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes the role of H⁺‑ATPase in mineral ion uptake by plant roots?
options: It creates an electrochemical gradient that drives the uptake of cations via symport
It directly transports nitrate into the root cells
It pumps K⁺ out of the cell to increase cytosolic K⁺
It is only active in the presence of mycorrhizal fungi
mcqs.explanation: The plasma‑membrane H⁺‑ATPase pumps protons out of the cell, generating a proton motive force that powers secondary active transporters (symporters/antiporters) for mineral cations such as K⁺, Ca²⁺, and NH₄⁺.

mcqs.question: In the apoplastic pathway of mineral absorption, which structure forces ions to cross a plasma membrane before reaching the stele?
mcqs.explanation: The Casparian strip in the endodermis is impregnated with suberin, blocking the apoplastic route and obligating ions to enter the symplast by crossing a plasma membrane.

mcqs.question: Which mineral is primarily taken up by a high‑affinity H⁺/phosphate symporter that operates optimally at low external phosphate concentrations?
mcqs.explanation: Plants possess a high‑affinity H⁺/Pi symporter (PHT1 family) that couples phosphate uptake with the proton gradient, especially when external Pi is scarce.

mcqs.question: Mycorrhizal association most effectively enhances the uptake of which mineral?
mcqs.explanation: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi extend hyphal networks into the soil, greatly increasing the surface area for phosphorus acquisition, the nutrient most limited by soil immobility.

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about the transport of potassium (K⁺) into root cells is FALSE?
options: K⁺ can enter passively through inward‑rectifying channels when external K⁺ concentration is high
High external K⁺ suppresses the activity of H⁺‑ATPase
K⁺ uptake can be coupled with H⁺ influx via a symporter
K⁺ is essential for maintaining cell turgor and stomatal function
mcqs.explanation: High external K⁺ does not suppress H⁺‑ATPase; the pump activity is mainly regulated by metabolic status and auxin, not by external K⁺ levels.

mcqs.question: During active uptake of nitrate (NO₃⁻) by root cells, the process is energetically coupled to which of the following?
options: ATP hydrolysis directly by nitrate transporter
Sodium gradient established by Na⁺/K⁺ pump
mcqs.explanation: NO₃⁻ is taken up mainly via H⁺/NO₃⁻ symporters that use the proton motive force created by the plasma‑membrane H⁺‑ATPase.

mcqs.question: Which factor most directly influences the rate of mineral absorption from the soil solution?
mcqs.explanation: Soil pH alters the chemical form and solubility of many minerals (e.g., Fe, Mn, P), thereby controlling their availability for root uptake.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes active transport from passive transport?
options: Active transport requires direct energy input such as ATP, whereas passive transport does not require energy
Active transport moves substances down their concentration gradient, while passive transport moves them up
Both processes always involve carrier proteins
Both are inhibited by low temperature
mcqs.explanation: Active transport is energy‑dependent (e.g., ATP hydrolysis) to move solutes against a gradient, while passive transport relies on the gradient and does not need cellular energy.

mcqs.question: In plant root cells, the uptake of potassium ions (K⁺) against a concentration gradient is primarily mediated by:
options: Simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer
Facilitated diffusion via a K⁺ channel
Primary active transport using a plasma‑membrane H⁺‑ATPase
Secondary active transport via a K⁺/H⁺ symporter
mcqs.explanation: The H⁺‑ATPase creates an electrochemical proton gradient; the energy stored in this gradient drives the uptake of K⁺ against its own gradient, classifying it as primary active transport.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is an example of secondary active transport in plant cells?
options: Uptake of glucose by a GLUT transporter
mcqs.explanation: The H⁺/sucrose symporter uses the proton gradient established by primary active transport to co‑transport sucrose into the cell, a classic case of secondary active transport.

mcqs.question: The movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane driven solely by a difference in water potential is called:
mcqs.explanation: Osmosis is the passive movement of water from a region of higher water potential to lower water potential through a semipermeable membrane, requiring no metabolic energy.

mcqs.question: Which statement about carrier proteins involved in passive transport is FALSE?
options: They undergo conformational changes to move the solute across the membrane
They can become saturated at high substrate concentrations
Their activity is directly coupled to ATP hydrolysis
They facilitate movement down the concentration gradient
mcqs.explanation: Carrier proteins for passive transport do not use ATP; they rely on the concentration gradient. Coupling to ATP hydrolysis characterises active transport carriers.

mcqs.question: In the pressure‑flow hypothesis, the loading of sucrose into sieve‑tube elements is an example of:
mcqs.explanation: Sucrose loading is driven by a proton gradient generated by H⁺‑ATPases, making it a secondary active transport process.

mcqs.question: Which condition would most likely increase the rate of passive diffusion of a non‑polar solute across a plant cell plasma membrane?
options: Increase in the concentration gradient across the membrane
Addition of a specific carrier protein
mcqs.explanation: Passive diffusion rate is directly proportional to the concentration gradient; a larger gradient enhances the net flux of the non‑polar solute.

mcqs.question: In the NCERT diagram of water potential (Ψw) in a plant, water moves from a region of higher Ψw to lower Ψw. Which part of the diagram represents the region of most negative water potential?
mcqs.explanation: The leaf mesophyll has the lowest (most negative) water potential because transpiration creates a strong water potential gradient, driving water upward from the roots.

mcqs.question: The NCERT diagram of plasmolysis shows a plant cell placed in a hypertonic solution. Which observation is correctly depicted?
options: Cell membrane shrinks away from the cell wall
Chloroplasts move towards the cell wall
mcqs.explanation: In plasmolysis the plasma membrane pulls away from the rigid cell wall as water leaves the cell, causing the membrane to shrink inward.

mcqs.question: In the NCERT diagram of the pressure‑flow hypothesis for phloem transport, loading of sucrose at the source causes which of the following changes?
options: Decrease in osmotic pressure in the sieve tube
Increase in turgor pressure at the source
Decrease in water potential at the sink
mcqs.explanation: Sucrose loading raises the osmotic pressure inside the sieve tube at the source, drawing water in and raising turgor pressure, which drives bulk flow toward the sink.

mcqs.question: The NCERT diagram illustrating the cohesion‑tension theory shows a water column in xylem under tension. Why does the column not break?
options: High adhesive forces between water molecules and xylem walls
mcqs.explanation: Adhesion of water to the hydrophilic walls of xylem vessels, together with cohesion between water molecules, maintains a continuous column despite negative pressure.

mcqs.question: According to the NCERT diagram of root pressure, which statement correctly describes the direction of water movement?
mcqs.explanation: Root pressure is generated when solutes are actively transported into the xylem, causing water to move osmotically from the surrounding cortical cells into the xylem.

mcqs.question: The NCERT diagram of stomatal regulation shows guard cells swelling in light. Which ion movement is primarily responsible for this swelling?
mcqs.explanation: Light triggers activation of H⁺‑ATPase, leading to K⁺ uptake into guard cells; the accompanying water influx causes the cells to swell and open the stomata.

mcqs.question: In the NCERT diagram comparing apoplastic and symplastic pathways, which pathway bypasses the plasma membrane?
mcqs.explanation: The apoplastic pathway consists of movement through cell walls and intercellular spaces, which does not involve crossing the plasma membrane, unlike the symplastic route.

mcqs.question: A plant cell has a pressure potential of +0.3 MPa and a solute potential of –0.5 MPa. What is its overall water potential?
mcqs.explanation: Water potential (Ψ) is the sum of pressure potential (Ψp) and solute potential (Ψs): Ψ = Ψp + Ψs = (+0.3) + (–0.5) = –0.2 MPa.

mcqs.question: A leaf loses water at a rate of 5 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹. If the leaf area is 10 cm², how much water is lost in one hour?
mcqs.explanation: Total loss = rate × area = 5 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹ × 10 cm² = 50 mg per hour.

mcqs.question: According to the pressure‑flow hypothesis, the phloem flow rate J = ΔP / R. If the pressure difference between source and sink is 0.4 MPa and the hydraulic resistance is 2 × 10⁹ Pa·s·m⁻³, what is the flow rate?
mcqs.explanation: Convert 0.4 MPa to pascals: 0.4 MPa = 4 × 10⁵ Pa. J = ΔP / R = 4 × 10⁵ Pa / 2 × 10⁹ Pa·s·m⁻³ = 2 × 10⁻⁴ m³ s⁻¹.

mcqs.question: What is the osmotic potential (Ψs) of a 0.01 M sucrose solution at 25 °C? (Use Ψs = –i C R T, R = 0.0831 L·bar·K⁻¹·mol⁻¹, T = 298 K, i = 1)
In the cohesion‑tension theory, if the tension in the xylem column is –0.5 MPa, what maximum height of water column can be supported? (Take ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
mcqs.explanation: Height h = |Ψ| / (ρg) = 5 × 10⁵ Pa / (1000 kg m⁻³ × 9.8 m s⁻²) ≈ 51 m.

mcqs.question: A root pressure of 0.2 MPa generates a water flow of 1 × 10⁻⁶ m³ s⁻¹. How many milliliters of water are exuded as guttation in 2 hours?
mcqs.explanation: Volume = flow × time = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m³ s⁻¹ × 7200 s = 7.2 × 10⁻³ m³. Since 1 m³ = 10⁶ mL, volume = 7.2 × 10⁻³ × 10⁶ mL = 7200 mL.

mcqs.question: Many students mistakenly think water moves from higher to lower solute concentration in plant cells. What actually drives water movement in plants?
mcqs.explanation: Water moves from regions of higher (less negative) water potential to lower (more negative) water potential, which incorporates solute potential, pressure potential, and gravity.

mcqs.question: A common trap is confusing the apoplastic and symplastic pathways for mineral uptake. Which statement is true?
options: Minerals enter the root cortex only via the apoplast
The symplastic route involves movement through plasmodesmata
The apoplastic route requires crossing the plasma membrane
Both pathways are identical in mechanism
mcqs.explanation: In the symplastic pathway, substances move cell‑to‑cell through plasmodesmata, whereas the apoplastic route follows the cell wall continuum without crossing membranes.

mcqs.question: Students often attribute root pressure to high transpiration. Which condition does NOT generate root pressure?
options: Active uptake of ions in the root
mcqs.explanation: Root pressure is produced by active ion uptake and water entry at night or low transpiration; high transpiration actually reduces root pressure.

mcqs.question: A frequent misconception about the pressure‑flow hypothesis is the direction of phloem transport. Which is correct?
options: Only upward from roots to shoots
mcqs.explanation: The pressure‑flow hypothesis states that sugars loaded at source cells raise turgor pressure, driving flow toward sink cells where sugars are unloaded.

mcqs.question: In hypertonic solutions, students often confuse plasmolysis with turgidity. What happens to a plant cell placed in a hypertonic solution?
mcqs.explanation: Water leaves the cell, the plasma membrane pulls away from the cell wall, and the cell undergoes plasmolysis.

mcqs.question: A trap in stomatal regulation questions is the hormone responsible for closure during drought. Which hormone causes stomatal closure?
mcqs.explanation: Abscisic acid (ABA) accumulates under water‑stress conditions and triggers stomatal closure to reduce transpiration.

mcqs.question: Students often misinterpret water potential signs. If soil water potential is –0.2 MPa and leaf water potential is –0.5 MPa, in which direction does water move?
mcqs.explanation: Water moves from higher (less negative) water potential (soil, –0.2 MPa) to lower (more negative) water potential (leaf, –0.5 MPa).

mcqs.question: A root cell is in soil where the water potential is –0.3 MPa. The pressure potential inside the cell is +0.2 MPa. What is the water potential of the cell?
mcqs.explanation: Water potential (Ψ) = solute (Ψs) + pressure (Ψp). Here Ψs = –0.3 MPa and Ψp = +0.2 MPa, so Ψ = –0.3 + 0.2 = –0.1 MPa.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly compares diffusion of CO₂ and osmosis of water vapor through a leaf stomata under high ambient humidity?
options: Diffusion of CO₂ occurs down its concentration gradient, while osmosis of water vapor occurs down its water‑potential gradient.
Both diffusion of CO₂ and osmosis of water vapor are driven by the same type of gradient.
Diffusion of CO₂ is driven by a pressure gradient, whereas osmosis of water vapor follows a concentration gradient.
Both processes are independent of external humidity.
mcqs.explanation: CO₂ moves by simple diffusion down its concentration gradient. Water vapor moves by osmosis (evaporation) driven by a water‑potential gradient between the leaf interior (more negative) and the humid air (less negative).

mcqs.question: Mineral ions often enter the root cortex via the symplastic pathway. Which situation most strongly favors this route?
options: When the Casparian strip blocks apoplastic movement, minerals must enter the symplast via carrier proteins.
When soil water potential exceeds root cell water potential, minerals move apoplastically.
High external salt concentration always forces minerals to use the symplastic pathway.
Abundant aquaporins make apoplastic diffusion faster than symplastic transport.
mcqs.explanation: The Casparian strip in the endodermis prevents passive apoplastic flow, forcing ions to cross plasma membranes into the symplast using specific transport proteins.

mcqs.question: According to the cohesion‑tension theory, what is the effect of a sudden drop in atmospheric humidity on the tension within the xylem column?
options: The tension reverses to a positive pressure.
mcqs.explanation: Lower humidity raises the water‑vapour gradient, increasing transpiration rate. Greater water loss creates a larger negative pressure (tension) in the xylem.

mcqs.question: In the pressure‑flow hypothesis, how does an increase in sugar concentration at the source affect the rate of phloem transport?
options: It increases the bulk flow rate of the phloem sap.
It decreases the bulk flow rate of the phloem sap.
It has no effect on the flow rate.
It reverses the direction of flow.
mcqs.explanation: Higher sugar concentration raises the osmotic (solute) potential, drawing more water into the source, raising turgor pressure and enhancing the pressure gradient that drives bulk flow.

mcqs.question: Which structural feature best distinguishes xylem from phloem in terms of transport directionality?
options: Xylem vessels possess lignified secondary walls, whereas phloem sieve tubes have perforated end walls called sieve plates.
Phloem cells contain lignified walls, while xylem cells have companion cells.
Both xylem and phloem have identical wall composition, differing only in sap composition.
Xylem transports sugars, while phloem transports water.
mcqs.explanation: Xylem cells are dead, lignified and form continuous vessels for unidirectional water movement. Phloem sieve tubes are living, lack lignin, and have sieve plates that allow bidirectional transport of photosynthates.

mcqs.question: A leaf transpires at a rate of 5 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹. If the leaf area is 200 cm² and the day length is 12 h, what is the total water loss from the leaf during the day?
mcqs.explanation: Transpiration per hour = 5 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹ × 200 cm² = 1000 mg h⁻¹ = 1 g h⁻¹. Over 12 h, total loss = 1 g h⁻¹ × 12 h = 12 g.
